illusory: Deceiving, or tending of deceive; fallacious; illusive; as, illusory promises or hopes.
illuminative: Tending to illuminate or illustrate; throwing light; illustrative. "Illuminative reading." Carlyle.
ileocaecal: Pertaining to the ileum and cæcum.
illiterature: Want of learning; illiteracy. Ayliffe. Southey.
ilmenium: A supposed element claimed to have been discovered by R.Harmann.
illation: The act or process of inferring from premises or reasons; perception of the connection between ideas; that which is inferred; inference; deduction; conclusion. Fraudulent deductions or inconsequent illations from a false conception of things. Sir T. Browne.
illuminator: 1. One whose occupation is to adorn books, especially manuscripts, with miniatures, borders, etc. See Illuminate, v. t., 3. 2. A condenser or reflector of light in optical apparatus; also, an illuminant.
illaqueable: Capable of being insnared or entrapped. Cudworth.
illimitable: Incapable of being limited or bounded; immeasurable; limitless; boundless; as, illimitable space. The wild, the irregular, the illimitable, and the luxuriant, have their appropriate force of beauty. De Quincey. Syn. -- Boundless; limitless; unlimited; unbounded; immeasurable; infinite; immense; vast. -- Il*lim"it*a*ble*ness, n. -- Il*lim"it*a*bly, adv.
illumine: To illuminate; to light up; to adorn.
illocality: Want of locality or place. Cudworth.
illimitation: State of being illimitable; want of, or freedom from, limitation. Bp. Hall.
illude: To play upon by artifice; to deceive; to mock; to excite and disappoint the hopes of.
illuminer: One who, or that which, illuminates.
ilvaite: A silicate of iron and lime occurring in black prismatic crystals and columnar masses. I'M I'm . A contraction of I am.
illicium: A genus of Asiatic and American magnoliaceous trees, having star-shaped fruit; star anise. The fruit of Illicium anisatum is used as a spice in India, and its oil is largely used in Europe for flavoring cordials, being almost identical with true oil of anise.
illustrious: 1. Possessing luster or brightness; brilliant; luminous; splendid. Quench the light; thine eyes are guides illustrious. Beau. & Fl. 2. Characterized by greatness, nobleness, etc.; eminent; conspicuous; distinguished. Illustrious earls, renowened everywhere. Drayton. 3. Conferring luster or honor; renowned; as, illustrious deeds or titles. Syn. -- Distinguished; famous;
illwisher: One who wishes ill to another; an enemy.
illegalize: To make or declare illegal or unlawful.
illiberality: The state or quality of being illiberal; narrowness of mind; meanness; niggardliness. Bacon.
illegitimacy: The state of being illegitimate. Blackstone.
illeviable: Not leviable; incapable of being imposed, or collected. Sir M. Hale.
il: . A form of the prefix in-, not, and in-, among. See In-.
illnatured: 1. Of habitual bad temper; peevish; fractious; cross; crabbed; surly; as, an ill-natured person. 2. Dictated by, or indicating, ill nature; spiteful. "The ill-natured task refuse." Addison. 3. Intractable; not yielding to culture. "Ill-natured land." J. Philips. -- Ill`-na"tured*ly, adv. -- Ill`-na"tured*ness, n.
illustriousness: The state or quality of being eminent; greatness; grandeur; glory; fame.
ilex: (a) The holm oak (Quercus Ilex). (b) A genus of evergreen trees and shrubs, including the common holly.
illabile: Incapable of falling or erring; infalliable. (old) -- Il`la*bil"i*ty, n. (old)
illfavored: Wanting beauty or attractiveness; deformed; ugly; ill-looking. Ill-favored and lean-fleshed. Gen. xli. 3. -- Ill`-fa"vored*ly, adv. -- Ill`-fa"vored*ness, n.
illtempered: 1. Of bad temper; morose; crabbed; sour; peevish; fretful; quarrelsome. 2. Unhealthy; ill-conditioned. (old) So ill-tempered I am grown, that I am afraid I shall catch cold, while all the world is afraid to melt away. Pepys.
illuminate: 1. To make light; to throw light on; to supply with light, literally or figuratively; to brighten. 2. To light up; to decorate with artificial lights, as a building or city, in token of rejoicing or… | To light up in token or rejoicing.
illegibility: The state or quality of being illegible.
ill: 1. Contrary to good, in a physical sense; contrary or opposed to advantage, happiness, etc.; bad; evil; unfortunate; disagreeable; unfavorable. Neither is it ill air only that maketh an ill seat, but… | 1. Whatever annoys or impairs happiness, or prevents success; evil of any kind; misfortune; calamity; disease; pain; as, the ills of humanity. Who can all sense of others' ills escape Is but a brute…
illusiveness: The quality of being illusive; deceptiveness; false show.
ilio: A combining form used in anatomy to denote connection with, or relation to, the ilium; as, ilio-femoral, ilio-lumbar, ilio-psoas, etc.
illutation: The act or operation of smearing the body with mud, especially with the sediment from mineral springs; a mud bath.
illustrable: Capable of illustration. Sir T. Browne.
illiteracy: 1. The state of being illiterate, or uneducated; want of learning, or knowledge; ignorance; specifically, inability to read and write; as, the illiteracy shown by the last census. 2. An instance of ignorance; a literary blunder. The many blunders and illiteracies of the first publishers of his [Shakespeare's] works. Pope.
illustriously: In a illustrious manner; conspicuously; eminently; famously. Milton.
illomened: Having unlucky omens; inauspicious. See Note under Ill, adv.
ilixanthin: A yellow dye obtained from the leaves of the holly.
ilium: The dorsal one of the three principal bones comprising either lateral half of the pelvis; the dorsal or upper part of the hip bone. See Innominate bone, under Innominate. [Written also ilion, and ileum.]
illy: Etym: [A word not fully approved, but sometimes used for the adverb ill.]
illative: Relating to, dependent on, or denoting, illation; inferential; conclusive; as, an illative consequence or proposition; an illative word, as then, therefore, etc. Illative conversion (Logic), a… | An illative particle, as for, because.
illecebrous: Alluring; attractive; enticing. (old) Sir T. Elyot.
illiterate: Ignorant of letters or books; unlettered; uninstructed; uneducated; as, an illiterate man, or people. Syn. -- Ignorant; untaught; unlearned; unlettered; unscholary. See Ignorant. -- Il*lit"er*ate*ly, adv. -- Il*lit"er*ate*ness, n.
illision: The act of dashing or striking against. Sir T. Browne.
illicit: Not permitted or allowed; prohibited; unlawful; as, illicit trade; illicit intercourse; illicit pleasure. One illicit . . . transaction always leads to another. Burke. -- Il*lic"it*ly, adv. -- Il*lic"it*ness, n.
illimited: Not limited; interminable. Bp. Hall. -- Il*lim"it*ed*ness, n. The absoluteness and illimitedness of his commission was generally much spoken of. Clarendon.
iliofemoral: Pertaining to the ilium and femur; as, iliofemoral ligaments.
illboding: Boding evil; inauspicious; ill-omened. "Ill-boding stars." Shak.
illume: To throw or spread light upon; to make light or bright; to illuminate; to illumine. Shak. The mountain's brow, Illumed with fluid gold. Thomson.
illatively: By inference; as an illative; in an illative manner.
illtimed: Done, attempted, or said, at an unsuitable or unpropitious time.
ileus: A morbid condition due to intestinal obstruction. It is characterized by complete constipation, with griping pains in the abdomen, which is greatly distended, and in the later stages by vomiting of fecal matter. Called also ileac, or iliac, passion.
illure: To deceive; to entice; to lure. (old) The devil insnareth the souls of many men, by illuring them with the muck and dung of this world. Fuller.
ileocolic: Pertaining to the ileum and colon; as, the ileocolic, or ileocæcal, valve, a valve where the ileum opens into the large intestine.
illogical: Ignorant or negligent of the rules of logic or correct reasoning; as, an illogical disputant; contrary of the rules of logic or sound reasoning; as, an illogical inference. -- Il*log"ic*al*ly, adv. -- Il*log"ic*al*ness, n.
illegitimation: 1. The act of illegitimating; bastardizing. 2. The state of being illegitimate; illegitimacy. (old) Gardiner had performed his promise to the queen of getting her illegitimation taken off. Bp. Burnet.
illiberalness: The state of being illiberal; illiberality.
illacerable: Not lacerable; incapable of being torn or rent. (old)
illustrate: 1. To make clear, bright, or luminous. Here, when the moon illustrates all the sky. Chapman. 2. To set in a clear light; to exhibit distinctly or conspicuously. Shak. | Illustrated; distinguished; illustrious. (old) This most gallant, illustrate, and learned gentleman. Shak.
illuminating: Giving or producing light; used for illumination. Illuminating gas. See Gas, n., 2 (a).
illuminati: Literally, those who are enlightened; -- variously applied as follows: - 1. (Eccl.) Persons in the early church who had received baptism; in which ceremony a lighted taper was given them, as a symbol of the spiritual illumination they has received by that sacrament. 2. (Eccl. Hist.) Members of a sect which sprung up in Spain about the year 1575.
illegal: Not according to, or authorized by, law; specif., contrary to, or in violation of, human law; unlawful; illicit; hence, immoral; as, an illegal act; illegal trade; illegal love. Bp. Burnet.
iliopsoas: The great flexor muscle of the hip joint, divisible into two parts, the iliac and great psoas, -- often regarded as distinct muscles.
illbred: Badly educated or brought up; impolite; incivil; rude. See Note under Ill, adv.
ileum: 1. (Anat.) The last, and usually the longest, division of the small intestine; the part between the jejunum and large intestine. [Written also ileon, and ilium.] 2. (Anat.) See Ilium. Note: Most modern writers restrict ileum to the division of the intestine and ilium to the pelvic bone.
ilk: Same; each; every. (old) Spenser. Of that ilk, denoting that a person's surname and the title of his estate are the same; as, Grant of that ilk, i.e., Grant of Grant. Jamieson.
illaudable: Not laudable; not praise-worthy; worthy of censure or disapprobation. Milton. -- Il*laud"a*bly, adv. (old) Broome.
ilicin: The bitter principle of the holly.
illstarred: Fated to be unfortunate; unlucky; as, an ill-starred man or day.
illtreat: To treat cruelly or improperly; to ill use; to maltreat.
illusionist: One given to illusion; a visionary dreamer.
illiberal: 1. Not liberal; not free or generous; close; niggardly; mean; sordid. "A thrifty and illiberal hand." Mason. 2. Indicating a lack of breeding, culture, and the like; ignoble; rude; narrow-minded; disingenuous. 3. Not well authorized or elegant; as, illiberal words in Latin. Chesterfield.
illusion: 1. An unreal image presented to the bodily or mental vision; a deceptive appearance; a false show; mockery; hallucination. To cheat the eye with blear illusions. Milton. 2. Hence: Anything agreeably fascinating and charning; enchantment; witchery; glamour. Ye soft illusions, dear deceits, arise! Pope. 3.
illapsable: Incapable of slipping, or of error. Morally immutable and illapsable. Glanvill.
illustrative: 1. Tending or designed to illustrate, exemplify, or elucidate. 2. Making illustrious. (old)
illness: 1. The condition of being ill, evil, or bad; badness; unfavorableness. (old) "The illness of the weather." Locke. 2. Disease; indisposition; malady; disorder of health; sickness; as, a short or a severe illness. 3. Wrong moral conduct; wickedness. Shak. Syn. -- Malady; disease; indisposition; ailment. -- Illness, Sickness.
iliac: Pertaining to ancient Ilium, or Troy. Gladstone. | 1. (Anat.) Pertaining to, or in the region of, the ilium, or dorsal bone of the pelvis; as, the iliac artery. [Written also ileac.] 2. See Ileac, 1. Iliac crest, the upper margin of the ilium.
ileac: 1. (Anat.) Pertaining to the ileum. [Written also iliac.] 2. See Iliac, 1. Ileac passion. (Med.) See Ileus.
iliad: A celebrated Greek epic poem, in twenty-four books, on the destruction of Ilium, the ancient Troy. The Iliad is ascribed to Homer.
illegible: Incapable of being read; not legible; as, illegible handwriting; an illegible inscription. -- Il*leg"i*ble*ness, n. -- Il*leg"i*bly, adv.
illumination: 1. The act of illuminating, or supplying with light; the state of being illuminated. 2. Festive decoration of houses or buildings with lights. 3. Adornment of books and manuscripts with colored illustrations. See Illuminate, v. t., 3. 4. That which is illuminated, as a house; also, an ornamented book or manuscript. 5. That which illuminates or gives light; brightness;
illuminize: To initiate the doctrines or principles of the Illuminati.
illuminant: That which illuminates or affords light; as, gas and petroleum are illuminants. Boyle.
illlooking: Having a bad look; threatening; ugly. See Note under Ill, adv.
illiberally: In a illiberal manner, ungenerously; uncharitably; parsimoniously.
illuministic: Of or pertaining to illuminism, or the Illuminati.
ilicic: Pertaining to, or derived from, the holly (Ilex), and allied plants; as, ilicic acid.
illapse: To fall or glide; to pass; -- usually followed by into. Cheyne. | A gliding in; an immisson or entrance of one thing into another; also, a sudden descent or attack. Akenside. They sit silent . . . waiting for an illapse of the spirit. Jeffrey.
illinition: 1. A smearing or rubbing in or on; also, that which is smeared or rubbed on, as ointment or liniment. 2. A thin crust of some extraneous substance formed on minerals. A thin crust or illinition of black manganese. Kirwan.
illegality: The quality or condition of being illegal; unlawfulness; as, the illegality of trespass or of false imprisonment; also, an illegal act.
illiquation: The melting or dissolving of one thing into another.
illinois: A tribe of North American Indians, which formerly occupied the region between the Wabash and Mississippi rivers.
ile: Ear of corn. (old) Ainsworth. | An aisle. (old) H. Swinburne.
illaqueate: To insnare; to entrap; to entangle; to catch. Let not the surpassing eloquence of Taylor dazzle you, nor his scholastic retairy versatility of logic illaqueate your good sense. Coleridge.
illusive: Deceiving by false show; deceitful; deceptive; false; illusory; unreal. Truth from illusive falsehood to command. Thomson.
illaqueation: 1. The act of catching or insnaring. Sir T. Browne. 2. A snare; a trap. Johnson.
illustration: 1. The act of illustrating; the act of making clear and distinct; education; also, the state of being illustrated, or of being made clear and distinct. 2. That which illustrates; a comparison or example intended to make clear or apprehensible, or to remove obscurity. 3. A picture designed to decorate a volume or elucidate a literary work.
illegitimate: 1. Not according to law; not regular or authorized; unlawful; improper. 2. Unlawfully begotten; born out of wedlock; bastard; as, an illegitimate child. 3. Not legitimately deduced or inferred; | To render illegitimate; to declare or prove to be born out of wedlock; to bastardize; to illegitimatize. The marriage should only be dissolved for the future, without illegitimating the issue. Bp.
illustratively: By way of illustration or elucidation. Sir T. Browne.
iliolumbar: Pertaining to the iliac and lumbar regions; as, the iliolumbar artery.
